fields.meta_description: Build a dental intake form that collects dental history and every insurance plan online, then flags answers before the exam. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Dental Intake Form Your Team Reads Before the Exam
fields.hero_description: Tell Emergent what your office asks new patients and which answers need a person. Emergent builds the dental intake form and sends each response to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What the Online Version Adds for Dentists
fields.features_subheading: Each one covers a job the front desk does by hand once a paper packet comes back.
fields.feature_1:
Dental history with real dates

Ask when the patient last had a cleaning and x-rays, and at which office. Problems like bleeding gums or grinding become boxes to tick, and each one opens a short note field.
fields.feature_2:
Medications listed one per row

List each prescription and supplement on its own row with the dose. Blood thinners and bone medicines get a separate yes or no question near the top, where the dentist looks first.
fields.feature_3:
Health answers routed to the dentist

Send a yes on a heart valve or a joint replacement to the dentist by email or Slack. The appointment keeps a flag until the dentist opens the answer and marks it reviewed.
fields.feature_4:
Subscriber details for each plan

Record the subscriber and member ID for every dental plan a patient carries. A second plan alerts your insurance coordinator on the same day the patient submits the form.
fields.feature_5:
Releases and policies signed on screen

Close the form with your financial policy and a records release, each signed by typing or drawing. Signed copies are saved next to the answers the patient gave that day.
fields.feature_6:
Code your practice keeps

Export the full code for the form and its database to your GitHub. A developer can run it on servers you choose or connect it to the practice management software you use now.

fields.usecase_heading: How Four Dental Offices Act on the Answers
fields.tab_content_1:
Old x-rays on order for the first exam

Bayview Family Dental asks new patients for their last dental office and roughly when their last x-rays were taken. The form ends with a records release. Once the patient signs, an email goes to the previous office asking for recent x-rays, and the chart shows the request as pending.
fields.tab_content_2:
Heart and joint answers wait for the surgeon

Health history at Northgate Oral Surgery asks yes or no about artificial heart valves and joint replacements. Any yes puts a premedication question on the consult for Dr. Owen Hale. Booking an extraction stays on hold for that patient until he reviews the history.
fields.tab_content_3:
Patients who rate their nerves 4 or 5 get extra time

Patients at Quiet Harbor Dental rate their nerves about dental visits on a 5-point scale and choose comfort options like headphones. A 4 or 5 books the first visit at 90 minutes. The options they picked print beside their name on the hygienist's schedule.
fields.tab_content_4:
A second dental plan caught when the form arrives

At Linden Street Dental, patients enter each dental plan with the subscriber's name and employer. Rachel Ames lists her own plan and her husband's. Two plans on one intake send an alert that day to Tasha Reed, the insurance coordinator. She confirms which pays first before the cleaning.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Dental Intake Form
fields.howto_description: Most of the work is deciding what the dentist must know before the first exam, and which answers someone has to act on early.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Collect the pages patients sign today
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask for every plan and its subscriber
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Mark answers the dentist must see
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pull together every page new patients fill in now, including anything handed over at the desk. Next to each question, note who reads the answer, whether that is the front desk, or the dentist. Cut the questions nobody has used in a year.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Give dental history its own screen, starting with the last cleaning and the previous office. Medical history comes next, with medications and allergies sharing one screen. Patients answer faster when each screen sticks to one subject and fits a phone without zooming.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Many patients are covered through a spouse or a parent. For each dental plan, collect the subscriber's details and a photo of the card. Let patients add a second plan without starting over, because the coordinator needs both to work out who pays first.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Choose the health answers that need a dentist before treatment, such as heart conditions or blood thinners. Name the person who gets each alert and pick email or Slack. Then decide what stays on hold, like booking an extraction, until that person signs off.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste your screens and rules into the prompt in plain English. Emergent builds the form and the database table behind it, with each alert set up. Change a question or a rule later by prompting again, and the live form updates.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 End with the release and policies
fields.howto_step_6_des: Add your financial policy and the consent to treatment after the last question, each with a signature field. A records release goes here too if you request x-rays from other offices. Have your office manager or counsel approve the wording before a real patient signs.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Run three test patients on a phone
fields.howto_step_7_des: Fill the form in as a patient with two dental plans. Do it again as someone who answers yes to a heart question, and once more as someone who rates their nerves a 5. Check that each alert reaches the right person and that card photos open.

plan.angle: Six of the eight results are dental offices posting their own packets (a general practice web form, a cosmetic group, a New Mexico PDF, the University of Minnesota dental clinic, an Irving office, a periodontist's referral PDF), plus a billing firm's explainer and one forms vendor. Every packet shares the dental-only sections a generic patient form skips: the responsible party and subscriber, dental insurance, last cleaning and last x-rays, gum and bite problems, and the health history a dentist screens for premedication. This page names what goes in each section and shows four dental offices where the online version acts on an answer before the chair: prior x-rays requested from the last dentist, a premedication question put in front of the surgeon, an anxious patient booked longer, and two dental plans sorted out before checkout.
tab_stories: A new patient at a family dental office lists the previous dentist and the date of the last x-rays, signs a records release, and the form emails that office a request for the films before the first visit.
An oral surgery practice asks about artificial heart valves, past heart infections and joint replacements, and any yes puts a premedication question on the consult for the surgeon to decide.
A sedation dentistry office asks new patients to rate their nerves from 1 to 5, and a 4 or 5 books a longer first visit with the comfort notes the patient chose.
A patient covered by her own dental plan and her husband's enters both subscribers, and the insurance coordinator gets both plans to check the day the form comes in.
